args.change: Make the 24 kHz playback path deadline-aware end to end: add a bounded 3-frame jitter buffer, sequence/timestamp checks, Opus packet-loss concealment, and a decode watchdog on the pendant. If a 24 kHz frame misses its 60 ms deadline or CPU headroom drops below a measured threshold, switch that utterance to a pre-negotiated lower-complexity/16 kHz fallback rather than emitting silence; report a typed audio-quality event to relay with packet loss, underruns, decode time, and fallback reason. Relay and Mac queueing must honor the event and avoid sending more concurrent audio jobs.
args.why_useful_to_owner: The owner should hear a complete, intelligible answer while walking through radio loss or a busy device—not a silent gap caused by a prototype path spending roughly 87% of one core on encode and decode. A graceful fallback is more useful than claiming '24 kHz' while dropping speech, and the telemetry lets the system improve routing without asking the owner to debug UART logs.
args.effort: Medium: firmware audio scheduler/buffer and Opus PLC work, relay event schema and transcoder negotiation, Mac/bridge queue backpressure, plus long-run RF-loss and CPU-load tests. Requires measuring actual available RAM/stack margins on the current DK before choosing buffer size.
args.risk: A fallback transition can sound different or duplicate a frame; sequence-aware crossfade and utterance-level mode changes limit artifacts. A bad watchdog could reset playback, so keep a kill switch and retain the current path behind a feature flag. Recovery is automatic re-negotiation on the next utterance and a diagnostic receipt if quality remains degraded.
args.cost_impact: No meaningful API increase; telemetry is small. Adds roughly 3×60 ms compressed-frame buffering plus metadata (likely under 10 KB RAM, to be validated against 211,608 B application RAM). Power rises slightly from buffering and telemetry; no new hardware required for the prototype.
args.latency_impact: Adds at most 120–180 ms startup buffering; no added latency after playback begins. Fallback prevents unbounded stalls and should reduce perceived latency during loss.
args.security_impact: Audio telemetry contains no speech, only counters and reason codes. Keep it session/job scoped and avoid uploading raw packets beyond the existing relay path.
depends_on: A typed end-to-end audio event/receipt schema shared by pendant, bridge, relay, and Mac.

Relay-side codec capability negotiation and queue backpressure.

args.security_concerns: Only inspect already-authorized private tabs/files and project the minimum conflicting fields. Never expose secret values in spoken prompts or relay logs. Identify sources by capability and timestamp, not by blindly trusting a website. Treat the owner's answer as scoped to the named entities and expiry window. Require confirmation before any irreversible action whose inputs were conflicted.

surfaces: pendant: capture the spoken time/energy constraint and deliver one short spoken recommendation
relay-realtime: clarify only if the constraint is ambiguous, then issue a signed triage request
mac-planner: inspect local reminders, notes, calendar gaps, battery/connectivity, and current work context
browser-extension: read already-open authenticated task/project tabs for urgent unresolved items, without opening new sites
relay: merge evidence, rank by deadline, consequence, effort, and interruption cost, and persist the decision plus expiry
pendant: play the recommendation and accept 'do it', 'defer', or 'show why'

args.latency_budget: Under 8 seconds when Mac and browser are already connected; up to 20 seconds if authenticated tabs must be reattached. args.security_concerns: Private calendar, reminders, notes, and authenticated pages leave their surfaces only as minimized excerpts and hashes. Do not expose secrets in the spoken rationale. args.change: Make 24 kHz playback the negotiated end-to-end contract rather than a decode-only mode: add a capability handshake (sample rate, frame size, jitter-buffer depth), a timestamped adaptive jitter buffer, and a CPU-aware half-duplex scheduler. During playback, pause/downsample uplink unless speech activity is detected; during capture, use the existing 16 kHz/16 kbps path. Add a measured fallback ladder (24 kHz → 16 kHz) and expose underrun, decode-time, and resampler telemetry in the receipt. Validate against the real I2S clocks and the ESP32 bridge instead of assuming the prototype wire rate is stable.
args.why_useful_to_owner: The owner hears a clear, continuous answer instead of clipped or delayed speech, while the pendant avoids spending nearly all of its CPU on simultaneous Opus encode/decode. It also makes the promised 24 kHz audio honest: when conditions cannot sustain it, the device degrades cleanly and says why rather than silently breaking.
args.effort: Medium-high: firmware audio state machine and telemetry, relay negotiation/transcoding changes, bridge clock validation, and an automated noisy-link/interruption test matrix. Requires an actual pendant/bridge bench run, not just simulator tests.
args.risk: A scheduler bug could drop a user utterance or leave the device in playback mode. Recover with a watchdog timeout to capture-only, a physical-button abort, sequence-numbered frames, and an always-supported 16 kHz fallback. Roll out behind a negotiated feature flag and retain current behavior for unknown firmware.
args.cost_impact: No per-request API increase; modest extra relay metadata. Engineering/test cost is the main cost. On current hardware no component cost, but a product revision may need a better I2S clock/amp (roughly $2–$8 BOM, negligible incremental power relative to the radio).
args.latency_impact: Adds one short capability exchange at session start; adaptive buffering targets 60–120 ms and should reduce retransmission-induced stalls. Half-duplex gating may delay uplink by a speech frame during playback, which must be surfaced in UX.
args.security_impact: Telemetry contains timing and quality counters only, not audio content. Capability negotiation must be authenticated to prevent a downgrade or malicious frame-size request; never log raw PCM or Opus payloads.

transcript.text:
Round 26 produced two new directions:

1. **“I have 15 minutes—what should I do right now?”**  
   A cross-surface triage capability that combines calendar, reminders, notes, authenticated browser tabs, deadlines, effort, and interruption cost into one recommended next action—with a deferrable alternative. It would use the pendant for the constraint and answer, relay for orchestration, Mac/browser for evidence, and require confirmation before any external side effect.

2. **Make 24 kHz audio a negotiated, resilient contract.**  
   The relay already renders 24 kHz PCM successfully, but firmware still needs capability negotiation, timestamps, adaptive jitter buffering, CPU-aware half-duplex scheduling, telemetry, and a clean 16 kHz fallback. This should prevent clipped playback and avoid saturating the nRF9160’s CPU.

I also confirmed the current blockers:

- Browser Bridge is offline, with **3 pending commands**.
- Mac Accessibility permission is still untrusted.
- Screen Recording permission is still missing.
- Computer-use vision upload consent is still false.
- The 24 kHz path has passed relay-side rendering telemetry, but still needs a real pendant/ESP32 bench acceptance test.
- The triage capability still needs durable decision records, normalized urgency/effort projections, and a cross-surface preflight.

The system has durable audio, pendant telemetry, persistent relay state, and Mac Bridge connectivity; the remaining work is making those pieces dependable together rather than adding another isolated feature.

args.change: Replace the prototype’s single-button interaction with a sealed, low-profile two-way tactile control: a three-position momentary rocker (left/neutral/right) plus a small haptic actuator, retaining the existing button as press-to-talk. Firmware should expose it as a signed, debounced event stream with press, hold, and release semantics; the relay maps those events to accept/defer/more-info, focus-mode changes, and safe transaction approval. Mac and browser surfaces consume the same event IDs and return a short haptic acknowledgement, so the control remains useful even when the voice link is unavailable.
args.why_useful_to_owner: The owner can make consequential choices quietly—in a meeting, on a walk, or when speech is inconvenient—instead of having to speak to the pendant or reach for a phone. A single left/right gesture can accept a prepared reminder, defer a decision, or reject an action, while haptic feedback confirms what happened. This gives the wearable a reliable control channel for the entire hive, not just a microphone and speaker.
args.effort: High: product enclosure and input redesign, electrical debouncing, low-power firmware event protocol, relay event persistence and replay, and Mac/browser handlers with receipts. Prototype first with an external wired rocker, then validate ingress protection, accidental activation, and glove use.
args.risk: The owner could trigger an action accidentally or misunderstand haptic patterns. Default every gesture to reversible/no-side-effect operations; require a deliberate hold plus distinct double-pulse acknowledgement for irreversible approvals; provide a physical lockout gesture and a voice escape. Event IDs, timeout expiry, and receipts make duplicate delivery recoverable.
args.cost_impact: Prototype hardware roughly $5–$15 in components and enclosure changes, with well under 1 mA average added draw for the actuator/input when idle and brief higher current during haptic pulses. No additional model/API cost for local gestures; relay persistence adds negligible storage cost.
args.latency_impact: Local acknowledgement should be under 100 ms. A remote action depends on the relay/Mac or browser, but the pendant can acknowledge receipt immediately and later signal completion or failure.
args.security_impact: Treat the rocker as an authenticated intent signal, not proof of identity: an unlocked or unattended pendant must not authorize purchases, sending, deletion, or publication. Bind approvals to a displayed/spoken summary, short expiry, action hash, and one-time event ID; retain only the event metadata, never ambient audio.
depends_on: A pendant firmware event protocol that survives dropped links and replays safely
Cross-surface action receipts and expiry-aware approval handling
A compact haptic vocabulary documented for the owner
A future product enclosure/board revision; the current Nordic development kit is explicitly provisional

I found a genuinely unfilled gap and recorded two proposals:

args.change: Introduce a signed Evidence-to-Effect (E2E) envelope shared by relay, faculty, Mac, browser, and scheduled jobs. Each envelope records observation IDs and redacted source pointers, timestamp/freshness, transformations and confidence, policy decisions, proposed side effects, approval token, and final outcome. The action runner must verify the envelope signature, scope, expiry, and revocations before every write; the relay can render a one-sentence explanation from it and the Mac dashboard can show the full chain. args.risk: Schema or signature bugs could block legitimate actions; recover by fail-open only for read-only explanations and fail-closed for writes, with versioned envelopes and a local emergency disable. args.user_asks: “I’m around people—keep helping, but don’t reveal anything aloud or on a screen someone can see.”
args.why_useful: The owner should not have to choose between privacy and assistance whenever they enter a meeting, shop, or transit. A spoken 'around people' mode would make the whole hive privacy-aware: the pendant stops speaking sensitive text, the relay classifies and redacts queued results, the Mac avoids displaying private summaries in prominent windows, and browser work continues but returns only minimal status cues. The owner can still ask for a discreet answer through a short button/voice interaction, and queued details become available automatically when private mode ends. This is a coordinated behavior change across all surfaces, not a mute switch on one device.
args.model_tier: Use deterministic sensitivity labels and policy rules for immediate redaction and routing; use a cheap background model only to summarize non-sensitive status. Realtime is reserved for the owner's short private query. No model should decide that secret content is safe solely from semantics without a policy label or explicit owner override.
args.latency_budget: Mode changes and output suppression must take effect within 200 ms locally on the pendant and within 1 second at relay/Mac. Status-only responses should be under 1 second; deferred summaries can wait until privacy mode ends.
args.cost_estimate: Negligible per mode switch; approximately $0.005–$0.03 for optional background classification of an unlabelled result. The dominant cost is implementation and testing of redaction/policy enforcement, not inference.
args.security_concerns: Default to withholding when sensitivity is unknown. Do not send sensitive text to the pendant while private mode is active; use opaque notification codes or haptics. Browser screenshots and Mac window content need separate redaction paths. Mode state must be authenticated to the owner's device, logged, and expire or require explicit exit so a forgotten mode cannot hide urgent information indefinitely. Emergency alerts need a configurable, minimal cue rather than spoken detail.

args.change: Replace the prototype’s 15,625 Hz capture path plus 31,250 Hz bridge-clock resampling with a negotiated 24 kHz audio contract: a microphone/ADC clocked at 24 kHz (or a dedicated low-power audio codec with 24 kHz mode), Opus 24 kHz capture and decode at 20–40 ms frames, and an explicit relay/ESP32 capability handshake. Add sequence numbers, sample-rate/clock metadata, underrun/overrun counters, and a loopback test mode; keep 16 kHz as a declared fallback rather than silently resampling. Move encode/decode work to a second audio-capable core/codec or budget a DSP path, because the current fixed-point Opus encode+decode already consumes roughly 87% of one core.
args.why_useful_to_owner: The owner gets genuinely wideband speech instead of a nominal 24 kHz playback stream fed by narrowband capture, with fewer glitches and an honest indication when the link falls back. args.effort: High: select and validate an audio codec/ADC, redesign clocking and bridge framing, update pendant firmware and relay transcoding, then run RF and battery tests. Firmware-only portions can land behind the capability handshake first.
args.risk: Clock drift, increased CPU/RAM use, RF bandwidth, and power draw could worsen dropouts or battery life. Recover by retaining the negotiated 16 kHz profile, gating 24 kHz behind a device capability flag, and refusing the profile when CPU headroom or packet-loss thresholds are unsafe. Validate with automated loopback and long-duration soak tests.
args.cost_impact: Prototype hardware roughly $5–$20 for a codec/ADC and clock/power changes, plus board spin; likely tens of mW additional draw depending on codec. API cost is negligible; 24 kHz Opus packets may increase relay bandwidth by roughly 1.5–2×.
args.latency_impact: 20–40 ms frames can reduce capture/playback latency versus the current 60 ms decode frames, but transcoding and clock buffering add a few milliseconds. Loopback diagnostics run only on demand or during commissioning.
args.security_impact: Audio remains the same sensitive data; diagnostics must never upload raw loopback audio by default. Send counters and hashes only, and require explicit opt-in to retain samples.

3. **Guided connection recovery** — the pendant explains the one permission or reconnect step needed, opens the appropriate Mac settings after approval, and verifies readiness before allowing queued work.

args.model_tier: Use a cheaper background reasoning model to build a bounded impact graph from current calendar, mail, notes, files, and authenticated pages; use realtime only to answer the owner’s spoken question and summarize the top two consequences.
args.latency_budget: Give a preliminary answer in under 5 seconds from cached state, then refine within 30 seconds if private browser or Mac sources need to be read. Never silently change a calendar, send a reply, or accept an invitation.
args.cost_estimate: Moderate background cost, dominated by retrieving and deduplicating private sources; one compact graph-analysis call per question. Reuse a short-lived impact graph for follow-up questions to avoid resending context.
args.security_concerns: This crosses highly private sources and may infer sensitive relationships or commitments. Keep source excerpts local or in encrypted relay storage, show citations and freshness, exclude secrets by default, and require explicit confirmation before any proposed change is applied.
missing: A temporal obligation-and-dependency graph that links people, commitments, places, documents, and deadlines across Mac and authenticated browser sources
A counterfactual evaluator that can compare proposed choices without mutating real calendars or accounts
A source-cited impact packet with confidence, freshness, and explicit unknowns
A compact pendant interaction for choosing among alternatives or asking one clarification question

args.user_asks: “Before you use another device or service, show me the smallest amount of my information you need to share, and let me approve or redact it.”
args.why_useful: The hive can reach private browser sessions, the Mac, a relay, and a wearable, but today the owner cannot see or control the boundary between those surfaces. This gives them useful cross-device assistance without requiring blanket trust or sending full pages, screenshots, transcripts, or credentials.
args.model_tier: Use deterministic field-level classification and redaction first; use a cheap background model only to summarize why each field is needed. Realtime reads a compact approval card, not the sensitive payload.
args.latency_budget: Generate a data-minimization preview in under 2 seconds for known workflows and under 10 seconds for an unfamiliar task. Once approved, execution proceeds without repeating the entire sensitive context to the realtime model.
args.cost_estimate: Low to moderate: classification and redaction are primarily local; one small model call for an unfamiliar data-flow explanation. Savings come from transmitting fewer tokens and avoiding screenshots.
args.security_concerns: The preview itself must not reveal redacted secrets. Store approvals as narrowly scoped, expiring grants tied to a job, destination, fields, and purpose; never permit credentials or secret values to cross surfaces. Destructive actions retain their separate confirmation requirement.
missing: A typed data-flow manifest for every tool and surface, including destination, purpose, fields, retention, and model visibility
Local secret/PII detection and reversible redaction before relay or browser transfer
A pendant-sized approval/redaction UI with deny, approve-once, and approve-for-this-job choices
Audit records proving exactly what crossed each boundary and automatic expiry of the grant

args.latency_impact: Battery state is local and immediate; relay trend updates within one beacon interval. No added voice latency except when the owner explicitly asks for a trend.

transcript.text:
This round I added three things:

1. **“What should I do next?” Now Card**  
   The system should combine current calendar, reminders, open private tabs, pending jobs, workspace state, deadlines, and available time into one ranked, reversible next step—not another list. It should prepare the step but stop before sending, buying, deleting, or submitting.

2. **Degraded-mode handoff**  
   If the pendant is offline, low on battery, or audio is unreliable, the relay should explicitly hand the task to the authenticated Mac/browser, preserve one idempotency key, and tell the owner what happened. No silent failure, duplicate execution, or false completion.

3. **Pendant fuel gauge**  
   The current prototype has no battery gauge. I proposed adding one, publishing authenticated battery/charging telemetry, and reducing LTE/audio activity before brownout so the owner gets an honest warning and retains an emergency-button path.

What is still needed before these can work end-to-end:

- Accessibility and Screen Recording authorization for the Mac agent.
- Reconnection and authorization of the browser bridge; it is currently offline.
- A durable cross-surface idempotent receipt/handoff protocol.
- A task-scoped, provenance-aware state snapshot API.
- A prepare-only action primitive with explicit approval boundaries.
- Final pendant battery/cell selection and fuel-gauge hardware design.
- End-to-end validation of the 24 kHz audio path, which remains the owner’s stated immediate priority.

The current live system still reports `permissions.ready=false`, so the Now Card and degraded handoff can be designed but cannot yet reliably inspect or act on the owner’s private Mac/browser state.

args.user_asks: “Privacy mode.” Make sure nothing is listening, recording, or reading my private screens until I turn it back on.
args.why_useful: A wearable assistant is present in intimate and public situations where software permission settings are too slow and ambiguous. The owner should have a physical, unmistakable way to make the entire hive go quiet and prove that it did so, rather than trusting an icon or a spoken promise.
surfaces: pendant: a long physical-button press cuts microphone capture locally, gives a distinct haptic/LED/audio confirmation, and retains the privacy latch across link loss and reboot
relay: immediately revoke active audio streams, cancel queued speech generation, mark the device privacy-latched, and reject new capture or private-context jobs
mac-planner/mac-vision: stop any in-progress screen observation, terminate or quarantine private-page extraction, and show a persistent OS-level privacy banner
browser-extension: revoke page-read capability and pause authenticated-tab commands until an explicit resume handshake
faculty-perception: verify each surface has stopped observing and report any surface that failed to acknowledge
faculty-judgement: prevent all plans requiring microphone, screen, browser, or private-memory access while latched
faculty-action: cancel or safely suspend pending work, preserving only a minimal non-content receipt so it can be resumed later
args.model_tier: No expensive model is required for the latch itself. Use deterministic firmware and relay policy; use a cheap background check only to reconcile acknowledgements. Realtime is allowed to speak the confirmation before the latch completes only if the local audio path has already been cut, otherwise use the LED/haptic confirmation.
args.latency_budget: Local microphone mute and physical indication under 100 ms; relay and Mac/browser revocation acknowledgement within 2 seconds. If any surface does not acknowledge, the pendant must still remain locally private and clearly show partial isolation.
args.cost_estimate: Negligible per-use model cost. A small amount of relay state and audit data; hardware cost is primarily a dedicated tactile switch or revised button/LED design, roughly $0.20–$2 depending on the enclosure and haptics.
args.security_concerns: The privacy latch must be enforced below the model and survive dropped links, prompt injection, and server compromise. Resume must require a deliberate physical action plus an owner-authenticated handshake; speech alone must not resume capture. Do not retain audio or screen contents created before the latch beyond existing bounded-retention policy. The owner needs a visible/haptic indication when any surface remains active or unverified.
missing: A hardware-enforced microphone power/capture gate and persistent privacy-latch state
A signed cross-surface privacy revocation protocol with acknowledgement deadlines and failure states
Mac and browser hooks that can stop observation rather than merely stop submitting actions
A privacy dashboard and receipt showing which surfaces are quiet, pending, or unverified
A resume handshake and tests proving the latch survives reboot, reconnect, and queued jobs

transcript.text:
Recorded a new capability: **physical, hive-wide Privacy Mode**.

The owner should be able to press and hold the pendant to immediately cut local microphone capture, revoke relay audio, stop Mac screen observation, pause browser access, cancel or suspend private-context jobs, and receive verified acknowledgements from every surface. Resuming must require a deliberate physical action plus authenticated handshake—not speech alone.

It requires a hardware-enforced microphone gate, persistent latch state, signed cross-surface revocation, Mac/browser cancellation hooks, and explicit reporting when any surface remains unverified.

args.subject: Cross-surface continuity
args.body: Yes: durable execution lease/idempotency is needed for Now Card handoff, especially disconnect/resume. I’m proposing a distinct user capability: conversation/task continuity after LTE or Mac/browser outage, preserving intent, partial evidence, and approval state without replaying actions.

args.latency_budget: On reconnect, local acknowledgment under 1 s; resume summary under 5 s after the first reachable surface. No action replay until the coordinator verifies the lease and asks again where approval is required.
args.cost_estimate: Roughly $0.01–$0.05 per interrupted task, dominated by background reconciliation and any regenerated summary; normal uninterrupted turns add no model cost.
args.security_concerns: The packet contains potentially sensitive spoken text, page excerpts, and draft fields, so encrypt it in transit and at rest, enforce per-task expiry, and redact secrets. Never infer approval from a stale packet; sending mail, purchases, deletion, and submissions require a fresh confirmation. A durable lease plus idempotency key must prevent duplicate clicks or submissions.

args.change: Make the 24 kHz path interruption-tolerant with a coordinated congestion controller: pendant-side VAD and Opus DTX suppress silent uplink frames; uplink speech packets get a bounded priority queue and sequence numbers; relay pacing caps downlink audio to the measured LTE-M budget, emits in-band loss/congestion feedback, and briefly switches to a lower complexity/bitrate profile when both directions contend. Keep a tiny rolling jitter buffer and explicit barge-in marker so the owner can interrupt instead of competing with playback. Validate with packet-loss, latency, and 60-minute battery tests before enabling by default.
args.why_useful_to_owner: The owner gets natural 24 kHz playback without the current failure mode where assistant speech causes roughly eight seconds of lost uplink. They can interrupt reliably, and short LTE contention becomes a tiny quality dip rather than a lost request.
args.effort: Medium-high: firmware queue/VAD/sequence work, relay pacing and transcoding, telemetry, and a hardware-in-loop acceptance harness. Requires revisiting the current 15,625 Hz mic/16 kHz uplink assumptions rather than pretending the path is already symmetric.
args.risk: Aggressive suppression or bitrate fallback could clip quiet speech or make playback sound worse; stale packets could be replayed after reconnect. Recover with feature flags, monotonic sequence validation, a fixed queue cap, and automatic return to the known profile after congestion clears. Preserve the SD failure-buffer policy—do not turn it into routine recording.
args.cost_impact: Near-zero per-call API cost; modest engineering/test cost. VAD and queue metadata consume some RAM, likely a few KB, while existing encode+decode already uses about 87% of one core. A product revision may need a more capable audio/DSP path if profiling leaves no headroom.
args.latency_impact: Adds approximately 20–60 ms of jitter buffering in the normal case; congestion fallback can add one frame. Barge-in recognition should remain under 150 ms.
args.security_impact: Sequence numbers and authenticated feedback reduce replay/injection risk. If VAD diagnostics are uploaded, send aggregate counters only; raw audio remains transient and SD remains failure-only.
depends_on: End-to-end 24 kHz playback acceptance tests
A relay/pendant telemetry schema for packet loss, queue depth, and barge-in
Confirmed Opus DTX and encoder controls in the vendored fixed-point build
A product hardware decision if the 87% CPU profile cannot meet worst-case scheduling

args.user_asks: “If something seems wrong and I stop responding, check on me in stages and get help without exposing my private data.”
args.why_useful: A wearable that can hear and speak should also protect the person wearing it when they cannot answer. The system would combine pendant-local signs (missed check-ins, an explicit distress gesture, or an unusual prolonged silence), relay availability, and the owner's calendar/location-free routine signals to decide whether to ask again, notify a chosen contact, or escalate. No single Mac, browser, or cloud service can provide this responsibly by itself.
args.model_tier: Deterministic rules and a small background model classify event combinations; realtime is used only for the pendant's immediate spoken check-in. No expensive model is needed for escalation decisions.
args.latency_budget: Local distress acknowledgment under 500 ms; first check-in within 10 seconds of a qualifying event; escalation stages separated by an owner-configured grace period (for example 2, 5, and 15 minutes).
args.cost_estimate: Usually under $0.01 per event for state evaluation and notifications; occasional background summarization is the dominant cost. Cellular data and SMS/voice escalation may add provider fees.
args.security_concerns: This is safety-critical and must never silently infer a medical emergency from ordinary quiet. Store only minimal event metadata, encrypt contact details, and require explicit opt-in, test mode, and a conspicuous cancel gesture/phrase. Never send calendar contents, page data, or location unless the owner separately authorizes it. Escalation contacts need signed, auditable templates and rate limits; emergency services should require a distinct owner policy and regional integration rather than an improvised model decision.

A secure notification/voice/SMS delivery integration with delivery receipts

args.user_asks: “Only interrupt me when it is worth interrupting me; otherwise queue it and give me one coherent update later.”
args.why_useful: Today each scheduled job, browser watch, and Mac event can independently compete for attention. This would combine urgency, deadline, confidence, current focus, and whether the pendant is being worn into one decision: speak now, vibrate later, queue silently, or suppress as duplicate. The owner gets fewer pointless interruptions without missing genuinely time-sensitive items.
args.model_tier: Background model classifies and deduplicates events; a cheap policy evaluator scores urgency and interruption cost. Realtime is used only when an approved event actually needs a spoken exchange. Pendant firmware supplies local wear/button/audio state; Mac supplies Focus/meeting/idle signals; browser supplies authenticated-page urgency; relay is the durable arbiter and queue.
args.latency_budget: Urgent safety/deadline events: under 2 seconds from event receipt to decision. Ordinary events: batch within 5 minutes or at the next owner-selected quiet-window boundary. Spoken delivery starts only when the pendant is available and the policy permits it.
args.cost_estimate: Approximately $0.001–$0.01 per event batch, dominated by background classification and optional speech generation; policy scoring and deduplication should be local/worker-side with no model call for obvious cases.

Never infer emergency authority from a low-confidence event. Require confirmation before any action, and let the owner inspect, mute, reprioritize, or delete queue items.

args.name: attention_arbitrate
args.why: A single durable arbiter is needed to decide whether cross-surface events should interrupt, defer, coalesce, or suppress. Without a typed decision endpoint, each scheduled job and surface will continue notifying independently and the proposed capability cannot be implemented safely.

input_schema.expected_output: A signed, explainable decision per event: decision (speak_now|vibrate|defer|queue|coalesce|suppress), deliver_after, expires_at, rationale_codes, grouped_event_ids, policy_version, and an audit record with idempotency key. It must fail closed for normal sensitive content but fail open for explicit deadlines above the urgent threshold.

args.name: offline_attention_latch
args.what_it_does: When the relay link drops or the owner is speaking, the pendant locally retains a small set of signed attention decisions already received (urgent, deferred, or queued), signals only the approved haptic/LED urgency pattern, and lets the owner press once to acknowledge or twice to request a compact replay when connectivity returns. It never invents urgency or exposes message text offline.
args.why_not_server_side: The decision may arrive just before a link drop and the pendant must avoid duplicate alerts or losing an urgent deadline while offline. Local acknowledgement and suppression need to survive radio gaps and button events.
args.trigger: Server push of an approved attention decision; link-loss/reconnect event; single or double button press.
args.inputs: Signed decision envelope: event ID, decision, urgency class, expiry, haptic pattern, acknowledge policy, and optional queue count. Local radio/link state and button events.
args.storage: Small ring buffer in pendant flash/NVS: up to 16 envelopes, event IDs, expiry, acknowledgement bits, and replay count; roughly 4–8 KB. No raw mail, page, calendar, or speech content.
args.ram_budget: About 8–16 KB working RAM including queue decode and debounce; bounded static allocation, no model or large text buffers, comfortably within the 211,608 B application RAM budget.

transcript.text:
Round 53 produced a new capability: **attention arbitration**.

The owner should be able to say:

> “Only interrupt me when it is worth interrupting me; otherwise queue it and give me one coherent update later.”

It would combine browser watches, scheduled jobs, Mac Focus/meeting state, and pendant availability into one decision: **speak now, vibrate, defer, coalesce, queue, or suppress**. I recorded both the capability and the required interaction-layer change.

I also requested:

- `attention_arbitrate` — a durable, explainable decision endpoint with deadlines, confidence, sensitivity, deduplication, and audit records.
- `offline_attention_latch` — a small pendant-side signed-event ring buffer so approved urgent/deferred notifications survive link loss without storing private content.

What I still need to implement this:

1. A shared event envelope and durable cross-surface event queue.
2. Pendant server-push, wear/speaking/availability signals, and local acknowledgement.
3. Mac Focus, meeting, idle, and audio-state signals.
4. Browser/job integrations that emit urgency evidence rather than directly notifying.
5. Owner-configurable quiet windows and escalation rules.
6. The current harness-ledger priorities and the actual 24 kHz audio implementation status, which remain unavailable to me.

Current live discovery also shows the home Mac bridge online, while the Chrome browser reports zero open tabs.

args.user_asks: “If I haven’t dealt with this by Friday, make sure the right person knows—but don’t send anything unless the conditions are actually met.”
args.why_useful: The owner can make conditional commitments without relying on memory. The system would watch for concrete completion evidence across the Mac and authenticated browser, remind the owner privately first, and—only under an explicitly configured rule—prepare or send a narrowly scoped escalation to a chosen person. This closes the loop between intention, evidence, and consequence rather than merely creating another reminder.
args.model_tier: A background model extracts the commitment, recipient, evidence criteria, and fallback wording. Deterministic policy evaluates deadlines and evidence. Realtime is used only for the pendant's brief confirmation or final approval conversation; no expensive model is needed for routine checks.
args.latency_budget: Commitment capture under 5 seconds. Evidence checks run hourly or at configured checkpoints. A missed-deadline decision should reach the pendant within 30 seconds; external delivery waits for explicit approval unless the owner has separately enabled that exact escalation rule.
args.cost_estimate: Roughly $0.005–$0.03 per commitment per week, dominated by occasional cross-surface summarization; most evidence checks are deterministic hashes, timestamps, and typed state reads.
args.security_concerns: Recipients, deadlines, and private evidence are sensitive. Store encrypted commitment definitions, minimize copied content, and show the exact evidence and proposed message before any send. Destructive or reputational actions always require confirmation unless the owner has granted a specific, revocable rule for that recipient and message class. Every escalation needs an audit trail and cancellation window.
missing: A typed commitment definition with completion predicates and fallback conditions
Cross-surface evidence adapters that can prove or disprove those predicates
A durable deadline monitor with timezone and clock-skew handling
A recipient-specific escalation policy and revocation mechanism
A review surface showing evidence, proposed message, and cancellation/approval controls

args.latency_impact: Adds roughly tens of milliseconds to a physical approval and negligible time to ordinary conversation.

1. **Conditional commitment handoff** — the owner can say, “If I haven’t handled this by Friday, make sure the right person knows.” The system verifies completion across Mac and authenticated browser evidence, reminds privately first, and prepares or sends a narrowly scoped escalation only under explicit policy.

args.user_asks: “Did that actually get done?” — after I ask the system to do something, give me a short answer about the real-world result, not merely whether a command was dispatched.
args.why_useful: Today an action receipt can say a Mac or browser accepted a command while the calendar, form, file, or message remains unchanged. The owner needs dependable closure, especially when they leave the room or lose connectivity. This turns the pendant into a trustworthy second check: it can say confirmed, not confirmed, or unknown with a reason and a link/evidence trail.
args.model_tier: Use the cheaper background model for post-action verification and evidence summarization; reserve realtime only for the owner's spoken follow-up and the final one-sentence answer.
args.latency_budget: Dispatch remains immediate; verify after a 2–10 second settle (configurable), then answer within 15 seconds. If a surface is offline, keep a durable pending check and notify when it reconnects.
args.cost_estimate: Roughly $0.002–$0.02 per completed verification, dominated by screenshots/DOM extraction and any model interpretation; typed checks should avoid model calls in the common case.
args.security_concerns: Verification must use least-privilege reads and preserve private-tab boundaries. Never infer success from a toast alone. Sensitive evidence should be hashed or redacted in receipts, and sending/deleting/purchasing still requires confirmation. Unknown must be an honest outcome, not a retry loop.
missing: A shared postcondition schema (expected entity/value plus observation recipe) across Mac, browser, relay, and pendant
Independent settle-and-reread verifier with idempotency correlation and PASS/FAIL/UNKNOWN states
A user-facing timeline linking the dispatch, observation, evidence, and any recovery/undo path
Reconnect handling for checks that were deferred while the Mac, bridge, or pendant was offline

args.change: Add a cross-surface postcondition verifier beside the existing action-receipt layer. Every planned action declares an expected typed postcondition (entity, field, target value/range) and an observation recipe (Mac accessibility/UI or filesystem read, browser DOM/session query, relay pipeline state, or pendant ACK). After a settle window, an independent verifier re-reads the target, correlates by idempotency key, records before/after evidence and freshness, and emits PASS, FAIL, or UNKNOWN. Queue UNKNOWN checks for reconnect and expose a compact evidence timeline plus recovery/undo suggestion.
args.why_useful_to_owner: The owner gets closure about what changed in the world, rather than false confidence that a button press was accepted. It is especially valuable for browser forms, reminders, files, and jobs that continue after the owner walks away.
args.effort: Medium-high: typed schema and receipt migration, four observation adapters, durable queue/reconnect logic, and dashboard/voice rendering; start with reminders/files/browser forms before arbitrary GUI tasks.
args.risk: Some actions have delayed or ambiguous effects, and UI reads may be stale. Mitigate with settle windows, source timestamps, explicit UNKNOWN, and no automatic retries for irreversible actions. If an adapter fails, retain the dispatch receipt and mark verification unavailable rather than claiming success.
args.cost_impact: Small storage increase per receipt (roughly 1–4 KB plus optional evidence hashes); background model cost only for semantic/ambiguous checks, with deterministic checks near-zero.
args.latency_impact: Adds seconds after dispatch for confirmation; immediate dispatch UX is unchanged. Offline surfaces defer verification instead of blocking the owner.
args.security_impact: Read-only verification inherits each surface's session permissions; redact secret values and keep raw screenshots/DOM out of voice and long-lived logs. Irreversible operations remain approval-gated.
depends_on: Existing receipt/undo records and idempotency keys
Typed context/provenance service or equivalent source/timestamp fields
Mac accessibility/browser bridge reconnect support
Durable relay job/event persistence

args.user_asks: “If this isn’t done by Friday at 3, remind me and prepare the next step.”

A conditional promise watches the actual postcondition, suppresses needless nagging when it is done, and escalates with a prepared reversible next step only when the condition remains unmet. This is a life-level safety net for applications, appointments, forms, and follow-ups.
args.model_tier: Cheap background/scheduled model evaluates the condition and drafts the next step; realtime is used only if the owner answers an escalation on the pendant.
args.latency_budget: Condition checks at a user-selected cadence or event, with a deadline-time check under 30 seconds; pendant alert should arrive within 5 seconds of a confirmed unmet condition.
args.cost_estimate: About $0.001–$0.01 per check when typed reads are available; model cost is dominated by drafting a next-step brief, not monitoring. Default to sparse checks and event-driven updates.
args.security_concerns: The promise definition must not expose private account data in notifications. Drafts remain unsent and destructive/financial actions require confirmation. The system must distinguish “not observed” from “not done” and avoid escalating on stale/offline evidence.

Postcondition verification adapters and freshness-aware UNKNOWN state

args.user_asks: “Notice when I keep getting stuck on the same kind of thing, and suggest one small change that would make it easier next time.”
args.why_useful: The system should improve the owner's life, not merely execute isolated commands. Across repeated pendant conversations, failed browser attempts, abandoned Mac jobs, and postponed reminders, it can identify recurring friction—without diagnosing or judging the owner—and offer a concrete, optional intervention at a calm moment. For example: “This is the third time the reimbursement form stalled at the same field; want me to save a private checklist?”

args.cost_impact: Low ongoing storage if sketches are capped and expire; roughly $0.01–$0.05 per scheduled analysis, with raw transcript/page retention avoided.
args.latency_impact: None for live actions; analysis is asynchronous and suggestion delivery is rate-limited.
args.security_impact: Reduces data exposure by retaining derived sketches instead of raw content, but the derived behavioral profile remains sensitive and must be encrypted, access-controlled, and excluded from ordinary prompt context unless the owner reviews it.

args.change: Replace the DK-era single-core audio path with a product audio design: a 24/32 kHz-capable digital microphone and an audio-capable dual-core MCU (or dedicated low-power DSP) with enough RAM for two Opus frame rings. Pair it with an adaptive full-duplex transport: 24 kHz superwideband by default, explicit uplink/downlink bandwidth admission, packet-loss concealment, and a deterministic fallback to narrowband before queue growth can cause multi-second speech loss. Add an end-to-end acceptance test that measures intelligibility, one-way latency, packet loss, and battery under simultaneous talk-over.
args.why_useful_to_owner: The pendant would sound natural and remain usable when both of you speak. Today the microphone is not actually superwideband and the radio/core budget demonstrably loses seconds of the owner's speech during talk-over; a codec label alone cannot fix that.

args.risk: A new board and clock domain can introduce power, EMI, and echo problems; adaptive downgrade could sound inconsistent. Recover with a hard codec profile version, feature flag, packet/clock telemetry, and keep the current 16 kHz path as a rollback until field trials pass.
args.cost_impact: No meaningful per-call API increase if Opus remains; prototype board roughly $30–$80 BOM increment, with a few mW to tens of mW additional audio/DSP draw depending on MCU.
args.latency_impact: Target 60–120 ms one-way audio plus bounded jitter; fallback must happen within 300 ms of congestion rather than waiting for seconds of queued audio.
args.security_impact: Audio remains TLS-protected; new telemetry should contain packet counts and codec state only, never audio. Firmware images and codec-profile negotiation must be authenticated.

args.user_asks: Tell me what I can safely ignore today, and keep anything risky from slipping through.

This gives them a finite attention budget: it separates harmless noise from items whose delay could cost money, time, or a missed commitment, then quietly defers the harmless items while preserving an auditable way back. It is a judgement service, not another inbox summary.

mac-planner/mac-terminal: read local reminders/notes and current focus state, and write a reversible daily triage artifact

args.security_concerns: Private mail/calendar/task contents leave the browser bridge only to the relay's authenticated job path. Never archive, delete, send, or change deadlines automatically. Require confirmation before muting an entire sender, changing a reminder, or suppressing an item beyond one day.

args.why_useful_to_owner: Instead of another long morning summary, the owner hears what is safe to ignore and can spend attention on the few things where delay matters. Low-value noise stays quiet without being lost, and every suppression can be inspected or undone.

transcript.text:
I found a concrete reliability gap: scheduled routines currently report `completed` even though the owner’s Gmail, GitHub, and Calendar reads have repeatedly failed. `GET /routines` exposes only an overall status, not source-level evidence.

I proposed a **routine coverage ledger and completion gate**:

- Track each required source as verified, stale, blocked, transient failure, or not run.
- Retry transient failures but stop retrying permission failures.
- Mark the parent routine partial or needing attention unless all required sources were verified.
- Deliver the same coverage receipt in the spoken briefing and dashboard.
- Never expose authenticated page contents or secrets in the receipt.

What this still needs:

1. A shared per-step receipt schema across scheduler, Mac, browser bridge, relay, and pendant.
2. Durable parent/child job state with leases and idempotent retry IDs.
3. Explicit required/optional source policies and freshness windows per routine.
4. Truthful Mac permission and browser-connection state.
5. A compact pendant rendering such as: “Calendar verified; mail unavailable; GitHub last checked 2 hours ago.”
6. Failure-injection tests for offline devices, stale data, permission denial, duplicate retries, and reconnects.

This is not a new standalone feature; it is the missing connective layer between `/routines`, `/jobs/:jobId/receipts`, browser sessions, `/briefing`, and pipeline audio.

transcript.text:
I found a remaining gap and recorded both a capability and implementation change:

### New capability: “Did that actually happen?”
After an action through the Mac or an authenticated browser, the system independently verifies the external effect—not merely that a click or command succeeded.

It reports:

- **Confirmed** — fresh evidence shows the intended state change.
- **Likely** — indirect evidence supports completion.
- **Pending** — the service has not settled yet.
- **Unknown** — verification could not be completed.
- **Conflict** — evidence disagrees.

The verifier would prevent automatic retries of non-idempotent actions, preserve scoped evidence, and send a short closure result to the pendant even if the owner has left.

### Stack change: External Effect Verification stage
I proposed adding an EEV stage between `/execute` and final job completion:

1. Compile an expected effect predicate for each step.
2. Dispatch through the existing Mac/browser tools.
3. Independently re-read the target state.
4. Correlate external receipts where available.
5. Persist a signed reconciliation result and evidence bundle.
6. Retry only explicitly idempotent operations.

This is connective work across existing `/plan`, `/execute`, `/jobs`, browser results, Mac actions, and relay status—not another generic action receipt.

### Still needed

No additional tool request this round. The implementation still depends on:

- Durable step-level job/event persistence.
- The signed state-witness protocol from perception.
- The action lease from faculty-action.
- Working browser-bridge reconnection.
- Mac Accessibility and Screen Recording permissions for independent observation.
- A typed effect-predicate and idempotency schema.
- A pendant result packet that survives a dropped link without replaying the action.

The key distinction is that current receipts prove dispatch; this would prove—or honestly fail to prove—the change in the outside world.

args.user_asks: “I got interrupted—pick up exactly where I left off.” The pendant should give me a 20-second resume briefing, reopen the relevant Mac document and browser tabs, and offer the single next step without repeating work or sending anything.
args.why_useful: Real interruptions currently erase the thread between a spoken intention, a private browser page, and Mac work. This would make the wearable a continuity anchor: I can leave a meeting, lose connectivity, or switch devices and return to the exact unfinished decision with evidence and a safe next action.
args.model_tier: Use the realtime tier only to capture the interruption marker and speak the short resume brief. Use a cheaper background model to compile the packet and reconcile job/session/browser evidence; use deterministic code for ordering, deduplication, and safety checks.
args.latency_budget: On the next pendant interaction, acknowledge in under 300 ms from a locally cached marker. Compile or refresh the packet in 2–5 s; if a surface is offline, say so and resume from the last verified checkpoint rather than blocking.
args.cost_estimate: About $0.005–$0.03 per resume, dominated by background summarization of changed evidence; near-zero when the cached packet is still fresh. Audio generation is a smaller additional cost.
args.security_concerns: The packet can expose sensitive page titles, mail, or documents, so store pointers and short redacted excerpts rather than full page content, apply per-source TTLs, and keep it device/owner scoped. Never replay secrets aloud by default. Reopening is reversible; any send, delete, purchase, or mutation still requires the existing confirmation gate. If evidence is stale or agents disagree, present uncertainty and ask one clarification instead of inventing continuity.
missing: A durable intent-continuity record with explicit interruption and checkpoint events across pendant, relay, Mac jobs, and browser sessions.
A resume-packet compiler that links the spoken intent to tab IDs, Mac paths, job IDs, receipts, and the last confirmed step, with freshness and redaction.
A local/offline pendant marker and reconnect reconciliation so an interruption survives a dropped link.
A one-tap/spoken “resume / discard / snooze” interaction and a dashboard showing packet provenance.

args.change: Add a durable cross-surface continuity graph and compiler. On every spoken task, browser command, Mac delegated job, and confirmation, emit a typed checkpoint event {intentId, sessionId, surface, object refs, step, status, evidence timestamp, sensitivity, expiry}. On interruption/offline/reconnect, deterministically select the latest verified branch, redact content by surface policy, and compile a small resume packet with provenance and one safe next action. Persist only refs/hashes plus short encrypted excerpts; make resume/discard/snooze idempotent.
args.why_useful_to_owner: The owner can stop mid-task and later say one sentence instead of reconstructing which tab, file, or pending job mattered. It prevents duplicate submissions and makes the system honestly say when a handoff is stale or incomplete.
args.effort: Medium-high: event schema and emitters in relay, Mac job runner, browser bridge, and pendant reconnect; compiler and retention tests; dashboard and voice interaction are moderate.
args.risk: Incorrect branch selection could resume the wrong task or reveal private context. Mitigate with explicit confidence, source timestamps, visible provenance, conservative no-op reopen behavior, and discard/undo. If a surface is unreachable, never infer completion.
args.cost_impact: Small durable storage and hashing cost; background compilation roughly $0.005–$0.03 per refresh, with caching keeping normal resumes near zero.
args.latency_impact: Sub-300 ms local interruption acknowledgment; 2–5 s network refresh. Cached packets make common resumes immediate.
args.security_impact: Cross-surface linking increases metadata sensitivity. Encrypt excerpts, scope by owner/session, enforce TTL and source-specific disclosure (especially browser/private mail), and keep secrets out of spoken summaries.

args.user_asks: “What promises have I made recently that I’m quietly failing to keep?” Give me a private, evidence-linked list of commitments inferred from my conversations, calendar, notes, and logged-in pages; rank the ones whose silence is most likely to hurt someone, and prepare a repair plan without contacting anyone.
args.why_useful: Today the owner can remember explicit reminders, but no system can notice the human commitments that were casually spoken or implied (“I’ll send that tonight,” “let’s meet next week”) and then compare them with what actually happened. This protects relationships and reputation without turning the assistant into an autonomous sender.
args.model_tier: Use a cheaper background model for nightly extraction and reconciliation; use realtime only when the owner asks for the private spoken summary. Deterministic code handles dates, evidence links, deduplication, and ranking inputs.
args.latency_budget: Nightly scan completes within 2 minutes in the background; an on-demand spoken answer starts in under 1 second from the cached ledger and refreshes in under 10 seconds if sources are online.
args.cost_estimate: Roughly $0.02–$0.10 per nightly scan depending on message/page volume; most cost is extracting candidate commitments. Incremental refreshes should be far cheaper through hashes and source cursors.
args.security_concerns: This is unusually sensitive social inference. Keep raw messages and page contents on the Mac/browser session, store only a redacted claim, source pointer, confidence, and expiry in the relay, and let the owner exclude people/accounts. Never present an inference as fact: say “possible promise,” quote the minimal evidence privately, and allow dismiss/correct. No message, reminder, or calendar mutation occurs without explicit approval.

args.why_useful_to_owner: It lets the owner repair neglected promises before they become relationship or work failures, while avoiding the false confidence and nagging caused by treating every thought as a task.
args.effort: High: new event schema, source adapters, entity/time resolution, deletion propagation, review UX, and extensive false-positive evaluation with owner corrections.
args.risk: Social inference can be wrong or invasive; a missed promise can be harmful, and a false accusation can be worse. Require evidence snippets and uncertainty labels, default to review-only, support per-person/source exclusions, and never send or schedule anything automatically.
args.cost_impact: Nightly background extraction approximately $0.02–$0.10 depending on source volume; local hashing/cursors reduce repeated processing. Storage is small if raw content stays on-device.
args.latency_impact: Background reconciliation in minutes; cached review list available immediately, with source refresh under 10 seconds on demand.
args.security_impact: High sensitivity. Keep raw content on the Mac or browser session, encrypt relay metadata, use short TTLs, honor deletion propagation, and do not speak names or evidence aloud until the owner requests the item.

Today that mismatch can look like a successful turn while the owner hears degraded audio or loses an utterance. This capability makes audio failure recoverable instead of silently conversationally expensive.
args.model_tier: Realtime model only for the short session-health decision and the owner's one-sentence alert; a cheaper background model summarizes diagnostics and drafts a bug report after the session. Firmware/relay contract checks are deterministic and do not call a model.
args.latency_budget: A preflight probe must complete in under 300 ms before speaking. On a mid-session fault, locally preserve the current utterance, announce fallback within 1 s, and resume via text or a re-established audio contract without replaying already acknowledged turns.
args.cost_estimate: Negligible model cost for healthy sessions; roughly one short realtime turn only on a fault, plus a cheap background diagnostic summary. Storage and relay overhead are small fixed-size telemetry records, not raw audio by default.
args.security_concerns: Do not upload raw probe audio or buffered speech unless the owner explicitly asks for a bug report. Send sample-rate/codec/sequence metadata and hashes by default; encrypt any owner-approved diagnostic clip, expire it quickly, and require confirmation before sharing it off-device or attaching it to an issue.

args.change: Implement an end-to-end AudioContract v1 negotiated per session: the pendant advertises capture clock (currently 15,625 Hz), encoder rate, frame duration, playback target, firmware build, and monotonic sequence; it emits a deterministic 20-ms probe and CRC/sequence markers. The relay must validate the contract against actual frame metadata, reject or explicitly label a resample instead of silently accepting it, and return a typed fallback reason. Add a 2–4 second circular compressed-frame buffer with an acknowledged-sequence watermark so one interrupted utterance can be retransmitted exactly once. On the current nRF9160, budget the buffer in external/flash-backed storage or reduce it to metadata plus the last unacknowledged utterance; do not pretend the 211,608-B application RAM can hold arbitrary PCM.
args.why_useful_to_owner: The owner gets an honest “24 kHz is active” guarantee—or an immediate, actionable fallback—instead of a conversation that appears complete but has mismatched capture/playback quality. A dropped link costs at most the unacknowledged phrase, not a required repetition of the whole turn.
args.effort: Medium-high: firmware framing and bounded buffering, relay schema/validation, bridge telemetry, integration tests with deliberately mismatched clocks, and a Mac diagnostic receipt. The existing 15,625-Hz microphone means true 24-kHz capture still requires a clock/ADC/bridge redesign; this change first makes the limitation explicit and safe.
args.risk: A retransmission bug could duplicate a phrase or increase modem airtime. Sequence/watermark deduplication and a hard per-utterance byte cap recover safely; if negotiation fails, use the existing path but announce degraded mode. A firmware rollback must understand both legacy and v1 frames.
args.cost_impact: No per-turn model cost. Small modem airtime increase only on loss; prototype firmware RAM pressure is significant because Opus already uses about 87% of one core when encode and decode overlap. A product revision with a native 24-kHz mic/clock is likely a modest BOM increase, roughly $3–$10, plus bridge/board redesign.
args.latency_impact: Adds under 300 ms once per session for probe/negotiation; steady-state latency unchanged. Recovery adds at most one frame window plus network RTT, rather than a full repeated turn.
args.security_impact: Metadata and CRCs are low sensitivity. Keep buffered speech encrypted and device-local by default; delete it after acknowledgement or a short TTL. Diagnostic uploads require explicit owner approval and must redact payloads unless requested.

args.user_asks: “Put me in a private bubble when I ask: keep sensitive answers and account details off nearby screens and speakers, let me review or act through the pendant, and automatically restore my normal workspace when I leave private mode.”
args.why_useful: A wearable assistant sits in rooms where other people can hear, while the Mac and authenticated browser expose far more than the owner intended. Today privacy is a conversational promise, not an enforced cross-surface state. A real private bubble lets the owner use the hive mind in public, at work, or beside family without leaking a password, medical detail, message, or account page through the wrong surface.
args.model_tier: Use deterministic policy and surface controls for entry, redaction, routing, and exit; use the realtime model only to classify the requested answer's sensitivity when no explicit label exists. A cheap background model may audit the session afterward, but must not receive raw private content merely to enforce the bubble.
args.latency_budget: Enter within 500 ms of a button press or explicit phrase, acknowledge privately through the pendant, and enforce screen/audio suppression before any sensitive result is rendered. Exit on explicit command or a configurable timeout, with a 1-second restoration budget.
args.cost_estimate: Near-zero model cost for explicit mode changes; occasional short realtime classification for unlabeled content. Main cost is engineering and OS/browser integration, not tokens.
args.security_concerns: The mode must fail closed: if the Mac or browser cannot attest that masking/muting succeeded, do not display or speak sensitive content there. Keep the mode state and sensitivity labels encrypted, do not log raw answers or screenshots, and require confirmation before opening the bubble to a new surface. A physical long-press should override accidental voice exit.
missing: A signed, shared privacy-mode lease with owner-selected sensitivity classes and expiry
Mac and browser adapters that can attest to screen masking, notification suppression, tab redaction, and speaker routing rather than merely claiming success
A pendant-local indicator and button gesture that work when the network is down
A policy engine that separates private answer delivery from private action execution and records only a minimal proof receipt

args.change: Add a physical privacy control to the product pendant: a latching microphone-power cutoff or hardware mute gate, a distinct haptic motor, and a two-color status indicator visible to the wearer. The control should generate a signed local mode transition even with no network; the relay and Mac must treat the lease as authoritative until physical re-enable or expiry. Do not rely on the current prototype’s single button/LED or on software muting alone.
args.why_useful_to_owner: The owner can know, by touch and without looking at a screen, that nearby people cannot be captured or that a private answer will not escape through the Mac. It remains trustworthy during a dropped link, crashed agent, or mistaken voice command—the exact moments software-only privacy fails.
args.effort: Medium hardware spin plus firmware, enclosure, accessibility testing, and relay/Mac attestation integration. The current nRF9160 development kit is explicitly provisional, so this belongs in the product design rather than being forced into its existing enclosure.
args.risk: A hard mute can interrupt an important request; provide a tactile acknowledge and a clearly distinct re-enable gesture. If the indicator fails, default to muted and report uncertainty on reconnect. Added components and enclosure changes require EMC, battery, and ingress testing.
args.cost_impact: Roughly $1–$4 in components at volume for a haptic motor, LED/light-pipe, and analog mute gate or switch, with transient draw under 20 mA and negligible idle draw; a redesigned mic/codec path could add more. No model/API cost.
args.latency_impact: Immediate local privacy transition (under 50 ms); no network round trip. Re-enabling capture may add one session handshake before speech resumes.
args.security_impact: Strengthens the trust boundary by making capture suppression physically enforceable. Signed mode events prevent a compromised relay from claiming privacy; avoid storing mode history beyond a short audit receipt.
depends_on: The shared privacy-mode lease and fail-closed policy from the proposed capability
Firmware support for an offline local mode state and signed event counter
Relay/Mac/browser attestation that the physical mode is honored

transcript.text:
This round I added three capabilities:

1. **Interruptible handoff** — “Pause this and come back later” saves the pendant audio position, Mac job, browser tabs, pending approval, and next action, then gives a short spoken resume brief.
2. **Guaranteed briefing delivery** — scheduled audio is tracked through generation, transfer, decoding, buffering, and playback; failures retry and produce a truthful missed-item receipt.
3. **Discreet mode** — a pendant-local latch suppresses private speech immediately, propagates a signed policy to the Mac/browser/relay, and fails closed while active.

I also proposed the firmware change for the discreet-mode latch.

What is still needed is implementation between existing primitives—not another permission request:

- A durable cross-surface handoff record and resume validator.
- Hop-level pendant playback acknowledgements and underrun telemetry.
- A signed safe-content/discreet-mode policy token understood by relay, Mac, browser, and audio playback.
- Server-side redaction gates that prevent private extraction or display, not merely private speech.
- Short retention and deletion controls for saved handoffs and generated audio.

Accessibility and Screen Recording remain unnecessary for these designs; AppleScript, browser sessions, relay jobs, and local pendant enforcement provide useful degraded paths.

args.user_asks: I lost my pendant. Lock it and revoke its access everywhere now—stop queued audio, invalidate browser and Mac control, and tell me what was successfully frozen. If it comes back, make me re-pair it before anything resumes.

args.security_concerns: Revisiting authenticated pages exposes only the minimum needed fields to the coordinator; retain hashes/snippets rather than whole pages. Never retry a potentially duplicate purchase, message, deletion, or submission automatically. Require confirmation before any retry or compensating action, and show the evidence source and timestamp.

transcript.text:
Round 66 produced a new integration proposal: **evidence quorum for important actions**.

The system should not treat a receipt, successful click, or HTTP 200 as proof. For consequential actions it should require independent witnesses—for example:

- Mac job receipt **plus** Calendar readback
- Browser confirmation page **plus** an authenticated record later
- File-write receipt **plus** content-hash verification

If witnesses agree, the pendant says **confirmed**. If they disagree or cannot be obtained, it says **pending/disputed**, creates a read-only repair ticket, and never blindly repeats the write.

I recorded both:

- A user-facing capability: *“For anything important, have two independent parts of my system agree it happened—or keep it pending and bring me the disagreement.”*
- An integration change connecting planning, execution, browser, journal, relay, pendant, and dashboard with typed states: `requested → attempted → witnessed → confirmed/disputed/expired`.

What I still need is implementation work, not another permission request:

1. A typed evidence-witness schema with source, timestamp, freshness, confidence, and correlation group.
2. Consequence policies deciding when one witness is enough versus requiring two.
3. Durable cross-surface claim/disagreement storage.
4. Readback adapters for Mac apps and authenticated browser pages.
5. Pendant/relay events for pending, confirmed, and disputed outcomes after link loss.
6. Owner policy for verification timeouts and which actions may never auto-retry.

The pendant hardware can support a compact offline status latch: its single LED/button and 211 KB application RAM are sufficient for a small pending/confirmed/disputed state, but the richer evidence remains server-side.

args.user_asks: “When I actually leave home, give me a two-minute departure check tailored to where I’m going—only interrupt me for something I can still fix, and keep the rest queued.”
args.why_useful: A scheduled morning briefing arrives at the wrong moment and a generic meeting brief does not know whether the owner has physically started leaving. This would connect the wearable’s real-world transition with the Mac’s live commitments and private browser context: catch the forgotten badge, medication, document, or travel change while there is still time to act, without turning every reminder into noise.
args.model_tier: Use a cheap event classifier and deterministic checklist first. Use a background planner to combine calendar, travel, and unfinished-job facts; reserve realtime for one concise, interruptible spoken alert.
args.latency_budget: Detect departure within 10–30 seconds; produce a first actionable check within 5 seconds of the event. Anything requiring authenticated browser reads can arrive asynchronously, with no blocking of movement.
args.cost_estimate: Usually <$0.003 per departure, dominated by one planner call and private-account reads; deterministic local checks should be free. Battery and cellular sensing are the main non-API costs.
args.security_concerns: Location and routine inference are highly sensitive. Keep raw location on the pendant or Mac, send only a coarse transition and destination class to relay, and make the feature opt-in with per-place quiet rules. Never announce sensitive calendar or health details aloud when others may be present; require confirmation before sending or changing anything.
missing: A reliable departure-event source: pendant motion/proximity/GNSS or a paired-phone geofence, with local privacy filtering
A destination and time-window resolver joining calendar, travel, tasks, and unfinished cross-surface jobs
A ranked 'still fixable before leaving' checklist with expiry and quiet/social-context rules
A low-interruption pendant interaction for dismiss, defer, or ask-for-more without opening the Mac

args.change: Add a low-power IMU and privacy-preserving local presence/departure detector to the wearable, with optional BLE proximity to the owner's phone or a home beacon and coarse GNSS only when explicitly enabled. Emit only state transitions such as HOME, LEAVING, ARRIVED—not raw traces—to the relay. Add a long-press gesture for 'quiet this departure check' and a short press for 'tell me the next item.'
args.why_useful_to_owner: The pendant would know when a real transition is happening instead of delivering a calendar briefing at an arbitrary scheduled time. The owner gets timely, location-relevant help during the small window when a forgotten item or changed reservation can still be fixed, without surrendering a continuous location history.
args.effort: Medium hardware and firmware change: select an IMU/BLE beacon strategy, implement local state classification and calibration, add encrypted transition events and battery testing, then integrate destination resolution and checklist ranking on the Mac/relay.
args.risk: False departures could cause nuisance prompts; require hysteresis, confidence thresholds, and a dismiss cooldown. GNSS and proximity data could reveal routines; default to local coarse states, disable raw logging, and provide a physical privacy mode. If the sensor fails, scheduled and manual checks continue unchanged.
args.cost_impact: Roughly $3–10 BOM increase for IMU/proximity hardware, plus firmware and battery tuning; likely tens of milliwatts peak and negligible average draw with duty cycling. No meaningful per-event model cost beyond the capability's planner/read costs.
args.latency_impact: Local transition classification in under 1 second; BLE/proximity transition typically under 10 seconds. Cellular/GNSS fallback may add 10–30 seconds and should not block the owner.
args.security_impact: Reduces data leaving the device by sending transitions rather than coordinates, but adds a sensitive routine signal. Encrypt events in transit and at rest, enforce short retention, and make privacy mode visible through LED/button feedback.
depends_on: A pendant firmware event channel and durable relay event schema
Destination/time-window resolver across Mac and authenticated browser
Owner-configurable quiet hours, places, and spoken-content privacy policy

args.user_asks: “Stop everything.” (or long-press the pendant button) should immediately silence the pendant, freeze new automation, cancel queued Mac/browser work, and give me a private receipt of what was stopped; “resume” should show the exact next unverified steps before anything continues.
args.why_useful: A person wearing an agent needs a physical, reliable boundary when a meeting starts, a private conversation begins, or an automation looks wrong. This is stronger than a conversational promise: it works during a dropped link, prevents queued actions from racing ahead, and makes trust recoverable rather than requiring the owner to remember which surface is active.
args.model_tier: No expensive model for the stop path; pendant firmware and relay perform deterministic cancellation. Use the cheap background tier only to summarize the stopped jobs. Use realtime only to speak the one-sentence receipt or ask for resume confirmation.
args.latency_budget: Local mute/LED state under 100 ms; relay cancellation and browser/Mac freeze target under 1 s when linked. Offline, the pendant remains muted and records a bounded stop marker until reconnect. Resume requires an explicit owner action and a short evidence/readback pass, not model deliberation.
args.cost_estimate: Near-zero API cost for stop/cancel; one short receipt generation is typically <$0.01 and can be omitted. Engineering cost is a firmware event plus authenticated relay fan-out and adapters for existing job/browser/pipeline stores.
args.security_concerns: The stop command must be accepted locally without network and authenticated on reconnect; it must not transmit microphone audio while latched. Cancellation should be idempotent and append-only, and receipts should contain job IDs/status—not page contents or secrets. “Resume” must never replay an irreversible step; it must require fresh preconditions and confirmation for send/delete/purchase.
missing: A pendant-local privacy latch with long-press debounce and persistent stop marker (single button/LED is available, but this behavior is not established).
A relay-wide freeze token checked by every new job/action and fan-out cancellation to Mac jobs, browser commands, and audio pipelines.
A durable stop/resume receipt schema that integrates faculty-action's requested/attempted/witnessed/confirmed checkpoint protocol and exposes the next unverified step.
A small owner-facing resume review UI/audio flow; macOS Accessibility remains unnecessary because cancellation can use the existing authenticated routes.

args.change: Add a pendant-local SafetyLatch state machine: a debounced 1.5–2 s long press enters STOPPED, immediately gates microphone capture and playback, flashes the single LED in a distinct pattern, persists only {epoch, latch counter, firmware version, reason=manual} in a tiny flash record, and emits one signed stop marker on the next link. A second deliberate long press never resumes automatically; it only requests a review state. Relay middleware should treat the marker as a kill token, atomically reject new work, cancel existing Mac/browser jobs, drain audio, and publish a receipt. Resume is a separate authenticated action after faculty-action verifies each checkpoint and presents the next unverified step.
args.why_useful_to_owner: The owner can create a private, quiet, non-negotiable boundary without finding the phone, speaking aloud, or trusting a network. If the link drops, the boundary still holds; when it returns, the system can explain exactly what did and did not happen instead of silently resuming.
args.effort: Medium: firmware event/state + flash record, relay latch middleware, adapters around existing job/browser/pipeline routes, and tests for link loss, duplicate markers, and interrupted irreversible actions.
args.risk: A false long press could interrupt a briefing, and a stale latch could make the agent appear dead. Use a distinct hold duration, LED feedback, explicit resume, watchdog expiry only for diagnostics (never auto-resume), and a local audible/LED acknowledgment.
